slides.title: The write decision: recall against noise

elements.text: The write decision: recall against noise
High recall, and a noisy store.
Every turn is stored: nothing is missed, and much of what is stored did not matter.
High precision, at the cost of recall.
Four ways to decide what is worth keeping.
The write decision trades recall against noise: writing everything gives high recall and a noisy store; writing selectively gives high precision.
FORMAT AND BACKEND ARE SEPARATE DECISIONS
Linked entities, and change over time.
"We moved serving from vLLM to SGLang."  /  "Uses SGLang for model serving."  /  {"serving_engine":"SGLang"}  /  Project -> USES -> SGLang
CLAUDE.md, scratchpad - easy to inspect, diff, search.
Redis, SQLite, Postgres JSONB - exact lookup, filtering, transactions.
pgvector, Chroma, Pinecone - exact or approximate similarity search.
Neo4j, FalkorDB (Graphiti) - relationship queries, multi-hop traversal.
The choice of representation and the choice of backend are two different decisions, made independently.

slides.title: Three usage policies: who decides to use memory

elements.text: Three usage policies: who decides to use memory
Predictable, but it adds latency and irrelevant context.
Selective, but it needs rules or a classifier.
Demand-driven, but it may miss useful reads or writes.
Many systems use a hybrid, and the read policy and the write policy may differ.

slides.title: The memory pipeline, and how it fails

elements.text: The memory pipeline, and how it fails
Seven stages: each one is a decision the designer has to make, not a default a database provides.
Forgetting is the stage students get wrong: without it, a stale memory silently overrides newer information.
Chance of an error-free run, at 95% success per step
The model assumes each step succeeds independently with probability 0.95. The deck notes that error propagation makes real runs worse than this model.
Reliability is arithmetic first, and attribution second.
A long trajectory is a reliability problem before it is a capability problem: 0.95 per step leaves 8% over 50 steps.

slides.title: Where does the failure come from?

elements.text: FIVE LAYERS, EACH WITH A TABLE OF MODES AND A FIX
Where does the failure come from?
ambiguous goal, proxy objective, unstated constraint, no definition of done, conflicting goals
context truncation, memory error, state corruption, control loop error, blocking fan-out
hallucination, instruction violation, faulty reasoning, reasoning-action mismatch, unverified success, long-horizon degradation
"requests.fetch() exists"; "undid its own fix from step 12"
truncated output, silent failure, ambiguous schema, flaky call, misleading error
the first 100 lines of a log missed an error on line 4,000; a date with no time zone scheduled a job 8 hours off; retried with sudo
stale state, version mismatch, random failure, rate limit
Python 3.8, not 3.12; HTTP 429 after 50 calls; leap year; redesigned checkout page

"We do not yet understand agents at scale, and there is little formal best practice." Designing for failure means bounding runs (step, cost, time caps), demanding evidence, failing loudly and pinning the environment.
Memory design is a chain of policy decisions: keep, format, store, retrieve, consolidate, forget.
Reliability compounds: bound every run and attribute every failure to one of five layers.
Valid time and provenance are part of the data model, not metadata you add later.
"We do not yet understand agents at scale, and there is little formal best practice."
The deliverable is a checklist of bounds - step, cost and time caps, checkpoints, typed schemas, pinned environments - not a recipe.
